To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

N mineralization rates after chemically killing managed grassland were best explained by the N content in the soil (hot-KCl extractable N) and the N content of roots and stubble, with a total of 62% explained variance.

the contents of total N and DOC are the best laboratory indices for N-mineralization after chemically destroying grassland, and that the N-mineralization rates are highest for grasslands that were killed in their early stage of succession.

N mineralization rates after chemically killing managed grasslands can vary from 0.3 to 3.5 g N m–2 wk–1 and are related to the total N, total carbon, hot-KCl extractible NH4+ and dissolved organic carbon (R2 > 0.38), while the dissolved organic nitrogen content was not related to the N mineralization rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of N mineralization rates in soils with a history of chemical destruction of grasslands.
a novel method to assess potential N mineralization after destruction.
the development and validation of indices for the estimation of N mineralization rates after chemically killing managed grasslands.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

indices of N mineralization rates after chemical killing of grassland can be improved by including the content of DOC and hot-KCl-extractable NH4+ in addition to the N content of roots, stubble and soil.
the N mineralization rates are best explained by a combination of several laboratory indices and the N content of roots and stubble.

the indices used are not very good predictors for N mineralization rates, but the combination of several indices and information about the grassland management can improve the prediction of N mineralization rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the N content of soil organic matter is a good predictor for the potential N mineralization after chemical killing of the grass, but the amount of N mineralized depends on the N content in the roots and stubbles as well.

the mineralization rates after chemically killing a grassland were mainly determined by the amount of total N, the amount of roots and stubble, the amount of hot-KCl extractible N and the age of the grassland.

N mineralization rates after killing grass with herbicides can be predicted with a reasonable accuracy by using information on the contents of total N and C, DOC, NH4+, and the N content of roots and stubble.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mineralization rates of grassland soils can be predicted from the chemical properties of the soil and the amount of organic N in the soil.
indices based on the C and N content of the soil are good predictors of N mineralization rates after chemically killing the grass.

the mineralization potential of grassland after chemical killing of the sward can be well predicted by a combination of several laboratory indices and information on the N contents of roots and stubble.
